title: Unrepresentative training data
description: The training set under-represents the population the system serves (regions, languages, age groups, minority classes), so the model performs worse for them and the gap is invisible in headline accuracy.
event: People in an under-represented group receive materially worse decisions or service
controls: A.7.4 data quality requirements; A.6.2.4 validation by sub-group; A.7.3 acquisition records
kri: Share of production inputs outside the training distribution; error gap between best and worst group
sources: MIT 1.3; ISO 42001 C.2.3; NIST AI RMF Map 2.3

title: Label error and inconsistent ground truth
description: Labels used to train or evaluate the model are wrong, inconsistent between annotators, or encode past decisions that were themselves flawed; the model learns the error and the evaluation certifies it.
event: Decisions built on flawed labels go wrong and have to be reworked or reversed
controls: A.7.4; A.7.6 data preparation criteria; A.6.2.4 independent test set
kri: Inter-annotator agreement; error rate on an audited label sample
sources: ISO 42001 C.3.4; NIST AI RMF Measure 2.1

title: Training data without rights or lawful basis
description: Data scraped, bought or re-used for training without a lawful basis, licence or the purpose it was collected for; the model cannot lawfully be used and may have to be retrained or withdrawn.
event: A regulator or rights-holder challenge forces the model to be retrained or withdrawn
controls: A.7.3 acquisition records; A.7.5 provenance; DPIA; A.2.3 alignment with the privacy policy
kri: Share of training sources with a documented basis and licence
reg: GDPR Art 5(1)(b), 6, 14; AI Act Art 10(2)(b), 53(1)(c); EDPB Opinion 28/2024
sources: EDPB Opinion 28/2024; Garante decision on ChatGPT, December 2024

title: Unknown provenance of a bought model
description: The deployer cannot say what the vendor's model was trained on; it cannot answer a regulator, a court or a customer about bias, copyright or personal data in the training set.
event: The organisation cannot answer a regulator, court or customer about what the bought model was trained on
controls: A.10.3 supplier process; A.6.2.7 technical documentation required by contract; A.7.5
kri: Share of AI suppliers providing the training-data summary and model documentation
reg: AI Act Art 13 (high-risk systems); Art 25(4) by written agreement for high-risk components; Art 53(1)(d) for general-purpose models; otherwise contractual

title: Input data drift
description: The data the system sees in production moves away from the data it was built on (new products, demographics, pricing, language), so outputs degrade while monitoring shows green.
event: Drift degrades outputs enough to disrupt decisions or service before monitoring catches it
controls: A.6.2.6 operation and monitoring; A.7.4; drift indicators with thresholds
kri: Population stability index; feature-distribution alerts per month
sources: NIST AI RMF Measure 2.6; ISO 42001 C.3.4

title: Missing, malformed or manipulated inputs
description: Upstream fields arrive empty, mis-coded or deliberately altered by users gaming a scoring model, and the model produces confident outputs on bad inputs.
event: Bad or gamed inputs produce confident outputs that are acted on
controls: A.7.4 input validation; A.6.2.6; A.9.4 intended use
kri: Input validation rejection rate; anomaly alerts

title: Over-retention and over-collection by the AI pipeline
description: Prompts, documents, transcripts and features are kept longer than needed or copied into vendor systems, widening the blast radius of any breach and breaching minimisation.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: AI data is kept longer, or copied more widely, than its lawful basis allows
controls: A.7.2 data management processes; A.7.6; retention schedule; vendor retention terms
kri: Volume of AI-pipeline data beyond its retention date; vendor retention terms reviewed

title: Uncontrolled access to training and feature stores
description: Engineers, contractors or the model itself can reach data sets holding special-category or confidential data without need; a quiet route to leakage.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: Unneeded access to a data store leads to leakage of special-category or confidential data
controls: A.7.2; A.4.3 data resources documented; ISO/IEC 27001 access control
kri: Privileged-access reviews completed on AI data stores

title: Fabricated facts, citations and figures
description: A generative model states things that are false but fluent: invented case law, policy terms, product facts, numbers; staff or customers act on them. False statements about named people can also defame them.
event: A fabricated fact, citation or figure reaches a customer, court or regulator and is relied on
controls: A.6.2.4 factuality evaluation; retrieval grounding; A.9.3 human review for consequential outputs; A.8.2 user information on limits
kri: Fabrication rate on a fixed test set; customer correction rate
reg: AI Act Art 50(1), 26(2); consumer protection law
sources: Mata v Avianca (US, 2023); Air Canada tribunal (Canada, 2024); Deloitte Australia report refund (2025); NIST AI 600-1 confabulation

title: Wrong decisions at the margin in scoring and classification
description: A classifier that is accurate on average is wrong for the cases near its threshold, which are exactly the cases where a decision matters (borderline credit, triage, fraud flags). Without a reliable confidence estimate on each output, nobody can tell which cases those are.
event: Wrong decisions on borderline cases cause serious harm to the people decided about
controls: A.6.2.4 threshold setting with the cost of each error type; calibration; A.9.3 human review band around the threshold
kri: Error rate inside the decision band; override rate
sources: Epic sepsis model external validation (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021)

title: Brittleness on edge cases and out-of-distribution inputs
description: Performance collapses on inputs unlike the training set (rare events, new formats, adversarial phrasing); the failure is total rather than graceful. Customers can also be left without service when the system refuses legitimate requests or answers with nonsense.
lifecycle: verification and validation; operation and monitoring
event: An unfamiliar input causes a total failure that stops or corrupts an operation
controls: A.6.2.4 stress and edge-case testing; A.6.2.6; fallback to a human path
kri: Out-of-distribution detection rate; fallback invocations

title: Unexplained variance between runs
description: The same input gives different outputs (non-determinism, sampling temperature, model routing), so decisions are not reproducible and cannot be audited or defended.
event: A challenged decision cannot be reproduced or defended
controls: A.6.2.4 reproducibility tests; A.6.2.8 logging of model version and parameters
kri: Output variance on a fixed test set between runs

title: Silent vendor model update
description: The provider replaces or retrains the model behind the API; behaviour changes overnight; validations, prompts and thresholds set for the old model no longer hold.
event: A vendor model change degrades outputs at volume before anyone notices
controls: A.10.3 contractual notice of model changes; A.6.2.6 regression suite run on every version; version pinning; A.6.2.8
kri: Vendor version changes per quarter; regression pass rate per version

title: Concept drift
description: The relationship the model learned stops holding: what predicted default, churn or fraud last year no longer does; accuracy decays while the model keeps scoring.
event: Decayed predictions cause losses, such as mispriced risk or missed fraud, before the model is recalibrated
controls: A.6.2.6 performance monitoring against ground truth; scheduled re-validation (clause 8.2)
kri: Accuracy on a recent labelled sample against the validation baseline

title: No defined metrics or thresholds before deployment
description: The system goes live without agreed measures of acceptable performance, so nobody can say it is failing, and the Act's testing duty is unmet.
event: A failing system goes undetected and an auditor or regulator finds no thresholds were defined
controls: A.6.2.4 verification and validation measures with criteria; A.6.2.5 deployment gate
kri: Share of live systems with signed-off metrics and thresholds

title: Evaluation on the wrong benchmark
description: Tested on a public benchmark or the vendor's demonstration data, not on the organisation's own cases, so test results do not predict production. Benchmarks the model saw in training, and models that behave differently when they detect a test, overstate performance in the same way.
event: Production performance falls short of what the tests showed and the shortfall disrupts the service
controls: A.6.2.4 test on representative held-out data of the organisation's own; A.7.4
kri: Share of evaluations run on the organisation's own data

title: Capability overstated by the vendor or the pilot
description: A pilot on easy cases persuades the business the system can do more than it can; it is rolled out to harder cases and fails.
event: A rollout to harder cases fails and the investment is written off
controls: A.6.2.2 requirements and specification; staged deployment (A.6.2.5); A.10.4
kri: Gap between pilot and production performance
sources: Amazon recruiting tool (2018); McDonald's drive-through order AI withdrawn (2024)

title: Agentic autonomy: actions no human intended
description: A system allowed to call tools, send messages, move money or change records acts on a misread instruction or a planted one; the damage is done before anyone looks.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: An agent takes an action nobody intended that moves money or changes records, with severe loss
controls: A.9.3 human approval for consequential actions; least-privilege tool access; A.6.2.8 action logs; a kill switch
kri: Actions executed without approval; blocked-action rate
sources: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (2026); OWASP LLM06

title: Interacting AI agents or algorithms produce outcomes none was designed for
description: Two or more automated systems, the organisation's own or other parties', react to each other: pricing or trading algorithms align or spiral, agents miscoordinate or loop, and one failure cascades through connected systems faster than people can intervene.
event: Interaction between automated systems causes a market, pricing or operational incident with material loss
controls: A.6.2.6 monitoring for interaction effects; A.9.3 circuit breakers, kill switches and human override; A.6.2.4 testing against other agents in simulation; A.10.3 interfaces with suppliers' agents documented
owner: Business owner of the automated process
kri: Circuit-breaker trips; unexplained correlated actions between systems
reg: MiFID II Art 17 (algorithmic trading); TFEU Art 101; DORA Art 6
sources: MIT 7.6 (V4 rows 63.01-63.10, 24.09.05, 56.11.00); the Flash Crash of 6 May 2010; OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications ASI07, ASI08

title: The system optimises a proxy for its goal, not the goal
description: The objective the system was given (clicks, handling time, approval rate, a reward score) diverges from what the organisation wants; the system games it, and the metric improves while the outcome gets worse.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: Optimising the proxy causes customer detriment or loss before the divergence is noticed
controls: A.6.1.2 objectives defined against outcomes, not proxies; A.6.2.4 testing against an independent outcome measure; A.9.3 periodic review of what the metric rewards
kri: Gap between the optimised metric and an independent outcome measure
reg: AI Act Art 9(2)(a); Consumer Protection Code
sources: MIT 7.1 (V4 rows 34.01, 35.04, 53.01, 54.03.01); Wells Fargo sales-target accounts (2016) as the human analogue

title: Defects in the system's design, code or data pipeline
description: A bug in feature code, a wrong join in the data pipeline, a mis-set parameter or an unsuitable model choice makes the system wrong in a way testing did not catch; the error is systematic rather than random.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: A defect produces systematically wrong outputs that are acted on before it is found
controls: A.6.1.3 processes for responsible design and development; A.6.2.3 design documentation and review; A.6.2.4 independent validation including code and data lineage; A.6.2.5 release controls
kri: Defects found after release per quarter; failed reconciliations of inputs to source
sources: MIT 7.3 (V4 rows 15.01.03, 15.01.06, 15.01.07, 19.01.02, 40.03.00); Knight Capital trading loss (August 2012); Post Office Horizon

title: AI acting in the physical world causes injury, death or damage
description: A system that moves, controls or advises on something physical (a vehicle, robot, medical device, building system or production line) fails or is misused and hurts a person or damages property.
event: An AI-controlled physical system injures someone or causes serious damage
controls: Safety case and hazard analysis under the sector standard; A.6.2.4 testing in the operating environment; A.9.3 human override and safe stop; A.8.4 incident communication
kri: Safety incidents and near misses per operating hour
reg: AI Act Art 6(1), Annex I (from 2 August 2028); Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230; Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745; Directive (EU) 2024/2853
sources: MIT V4 rows 58.02, 66.11; Uber test vehicle fatality, Tempe (March 2018); Cruise (October 2023)

title: Discriminatory outcomes in hiring and worker management
description: Screening, ranking or monitoring tools penalise applicants or staff by sex, age, disability, ethnicity or proxies of them; claims, regulator action and reputational damage follow.
event: A hiring or worker tool disadvantages people on a protected ground
controls: A.5.4 impact assessment on individuals; A.6.2.4 bias testing by group before and after deployment; A.9.3
kri: Selection-rate ratios by group; complaints alleging bias
reg: AI Act Annex III(4), Art 10(2)(f), 26(7); Employment Equality Acts; NYC Local Law 144; Illinois HB 3773
sources: Amazon recruiting tool (2018); iTutorGroup EEOC settlement (2023); Mobley v Workday (US, ongoing)

title: Discriminatory outcomes in credit, insurance and pricing
description: Creditworthiness or pricing models disadvantage protected groups directly or through proxies (postcode, device, name).
event: A credit or pricing model disadvantages a protected group
controls: A.5.4; fairness metrics with thresholds; adverse-action explanations; A.9.3
kri: Approval-rate and price gaps by group after controlling for risk
reg: AI Act Annex III(5)(b),(c), Art 27; Equal Status Acts; Consumer Protection Code
sources: Apple Card inquiry by New York DFS (2019-2021)

title: Discriminatory outcomes in public services and benefits
description: Eligibility, fraud-risk or triage models in public bodies single out groups (nationality, ethnicity, low income) for scrutiny or denial.
event: A group is wrongly singled out for scrutiny or denied a public service
controls: A.5.4, A.5.5; fundamental rights impact assessment (Art 27) before use; human decision on adverse outcomes; A.8.3 complaints channel
kri: Scrutiny rates by group; overturn rate on appeal
reg: AI Act Annex III(5)(a), Art 27; GDPR Art 22
sources: Dutch childcare benefits scandal (2021); Robodebt Royal Commission (2023); SyRI judgment (The Hague, 2020)

title: Unequal accuracy across groups
description: Face, voice, language or medical models perform worse for darker skin, accents, dialects, women or older people; the errors fall on those groups.
lifecycle: verification and validation; operation and monitoring
event: A group suffers serious harm from the system's higher error rate for them
controls: A.6.2.4 disaggregated evaluation; A.7.4 representative data; A.8.2 limits disclosed to users
kri: Accuracy gap between the best and worst performing group
sources: FTC order against Rite Aid (2023); Gender Shades study (2018)

title: Proxy variables and feedback loops
description: Innocuous features stand in for protected ones, and the model's own decisions generate the next training data (more scrutiny, fewer loans), entrenching the pattern.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: A proxy-driven pattern entrenches and causes serious harm to a group
controls: Feature review for proxies (A.7.6); A.6.2.4; periodic re-identification (8.2); A.5.5 societal impact
kri: Proxy-correlation audit results; drift in group outcomes across cycles

title: Toxic or demeaning outputs under the organisation's brand
description: A chatbot or content tool produces abusive, sexual, extremist or demeaning material, or is manipulated into it, in the organisation's name.
event: A toxic or demeaning output reaches a user in the organisation's name
controls: Content filters and red-teaming (A.6.2.4); A.9.4 intended use; monitoring and takedown (A.6.2.6); A.8.4 incident communication
kri: Flagged-output rate; time to takedown
reg: AI Act Art 50; Digital Services Act; UK Online Safety Act

title: Generated content stereotypes, erases or misrepresents groups
description: Text, images or voice produced by the organisation's system repeat stereotypes, leave groups out or portray them falsely (in marketing, recruitment material or customer answers), although no single decision is discriminatory.
event: Stereotyped or exclusionary content is published under the organisation's name
controls: A.6.2.4 testing of generated content for representation by group; A.9.3 review of content before publication; A.5.4 impact assessment on affected groups
kri: Share of sampled outputs failing the representation checklist; complaints about stereotyping
reg: Equal Status Acts 2000-2018; Employment Equality Acts (recruitment material); AI Act Art 50
sources: MIT 1.1 (V4 rows 04.02, 11.01, 16.01); Google suspended Gemini image generation of people (February 2024)

title: Affected people are not told an AI system is used on them
description: Customers, applicants or citizens are not informed that a decision was made or assisted by AI, so they cannot question it; where the Act's or the GDPR's notice duties apply, that is a breach.
event: People are not told that AI is used on them where the law requires it
controls: A.8.2 user information; A.8.5 obligations to interested parties; privacy notices; Art 26(11) notice
kri: Share of AI-assisted decisions carrying a notice; complaints citing no notice

title: No meaningful explanation or route to contest
description: A person refused credit, a job, housing or a benefit cannot get a reason a human can act on, nor a human review; the organisation cannot defend the decision either.
event: A refused person gets no explanation or review, and a wrong decision stands
controls: Explanation capability specified (A.6.2.2); A.9.3 human review with authority to override; A.8.3 reporting channel
kri: Explanation requests; outcomes of human review

title: The organisation cannot explain its own model
description: Nobody inside can say which features drive the output, so errors cannot be diagnosed, bias cannot be traced and the regulator cannot be answered.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: The organisation cannot answer a regulator or diagnose an error when asked
controls: A.6.2.3 design documentation; interpretability methods in validation (A.6.2.4); A.6.2.7 technical documentation
kri: Documentation completeness score per system

title: Vendor opacity
description: The supplier refuses or cannot provide model cards, evaluation results, training-data summaries or incident history; the deployer carries the risk blind.
event: The deployer cannot answer a regulator, auditor or customer about the vendor's model
controls: A.10.3 supplier requirements; A.6.2.7 documentation as a contract condition; Art 13 and 25 information rights
kri: Share of AI contracts with documentation and notification clauses
reg: AI Act Art 13 (high-risk systems); Art 25(4) by written agreement for high-risk components; Art 53 for general-purpose models; otherwise contractual

title: No named owner for the AI system or its decisions
description: The model belongs to IT or to the vendor; when it fails nobody is accountable, nobody re-assesses it, and the inventory line goes stale.
event: A failure goes unaddressed because nobody owns the system
controls: A.3.2 roles and responsibilities; A.10.2 allocation with third parties; inventory with a named owner
kri: Share of inventory lines with a named, current owner
reg: AI Act Art 26(2), 25; GDPR Art 5(2) accountability

title: Decisions laundered through the machine
description: Staff attribute their own decisions to the system, or the system's output is treated as a decision no human took; accountability dissolves.
event: A harmful decision is not corrected because nobody accepts it as theirs
controls: A.9.3 oversight objectives with decision rights; A.3.3 reporting of concerns; training (7.2)
kri: Override and challenge rates; complaint analysis

title: No logs, or logs that cannot reconstruct a decision
description: The system does not record inputs, version, parameters and outputs in a way that lets anyone reconstruct what happened; logging duties are unmet and incidents cannot be investigated.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: An incident or complaint cannot be investigated, or a decision reconstructed, when required
controls: A.6.2.8 event logs; A.5.3 retention of assessments; log retention policy (six months minimum for deployers)
kri: Share of systems with reconstructable logs; log-retention compliance

title: Documentation that does not match the system in production
description: Technical files, risk assessments and user instructions describe a version that no longer runs; the record is a liability rather than a defence.
event: An auditor or regulator relies on documentation that describes a superseded version
controls: 7.5 control of documented information; change-triggered re-documentation (6.3); A.6.2.7
kri: Documentation age against the last model change

title: Automation bias: operators accept outputs they should question
description: Reviewers approve the machine's recommendation at a rate that shows no review is taking place; errors flow through unchecked while the oversight box is ticked.
event: Errors approved by reviewers reach people and cause them serious harm
controls: A.9.3 oversight design with sampling and blind re-checks; training on failure modes; override-rate monitoring; Art 14(4)(b) awareness
kri: Override rate; agreement with the model on a blind sample
sources: Epic sepsis model (2021); Post Office Horizon (UK)

title: Over-reliance on generative output in professional work
description: Lawyers, clinicians, advisers and engineers submit AI-produced work without checking; fabrications and errors reach clients, courts and regulators.
event: An unchecked AI-produced error reaches a client, court or regulator and is relied on
controls: Acceptable-use policy (A.2.2, A.9.2); mandatory verification of external outputs; training (7.2, Art 4)
kri: Sampled error rate in AI-assisted deliverables
reg: AI Act Art 4; professional codes of conduct

title: Use outside the intended purpose
description: A tool procured for drafting is used for decisions; a model built for one population is run on another; a triage aid becomes the decider.
event: A tool used beyond its purpose causes serious harm to the people it is used on
controls: A.9.4 intended use enforced; A.9.2 processes for use; A.6.2.5 deployment plan; use-case inventory
kri: Uses in production not in the inventory; mismatches found in review

title: Reasonably foreseeable misuse by users
description: Customers or staff use the system for ends it was not designed for (medical advice from a sales bot, harassment through an image tool); the organisation answers for what it should have foreseen.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: Users misuse the system in a way that causes harm the organisation answers for
controls: A.5.2 impact assessment covering misuse (ISO/IEC 42005 6.8.3); guardrails; A.8.2 user information; monitoring
kri: Blocked misuse attempts; incident reports

title: Operators lack the competence to oversee
description: The people assigned to oversee the system do not understand its limits, its failure modes or their authority; oversight exists on paper only.
event: An overseer fails to catch or stop an error that seriously harms someone
controls: 7.2 competence; A.4.6 human resources documented; Art 4 literacy programme; role-specific training
kri: Share of overseers trained and assessed; literacy coverage

title: Deskilling and loss of institutional knowledge
description: After years of the machine doing the task, nobody can do it by hand, check the output or run the service when the system fails.
event: When the system fails, nobody can run the service or check the output by hand
controls: A.4.6; rotation and manual-run exercises; continuity plans (A.6.2.6)
kri: Manual-capability drills passed; key-person dependence

title: Oversight that cannot override, or that nobody uses
description: The interface gives the reviewer no way to stop or change the output, or the volume makes review impossible (alert fatigue); the human in the loop is decoration.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: Reviewers cannot stop an error at volume and it seriously harms people
controls: A.9.3 override authority and tooling; workload design; alert thresholds tuned; Art 14(3) measures built in by the provider
kri: Alerts per reviewer per day; actions taken on alerts

title: Manipulation, dark patterns and emotional dependence
description: Conversational systems nudge, deceive or form attachments with users (children, vulnerable adults, lonely customers) in ways that damage them or breach the Act's prohibitions. Sycophancy, telling users what they want to hear, is one form.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: A conversational system damages a vulnerable user or breaches a prohibition
controls: A.5.4 impact on vulnerable groups; design reviews; A.9.3; age assurance; Art 5 screening at classification
kri: Vulnerable-user interaction metrics; complaints

title: The system gives users practical help to cause harm
description: A chatbot or assistant gives a user workable instructions or encouragement for crime, violence, weapons, fraud or self-harm, in the organisation's name or through its product.
event: Help given by the system contributes to a crime, an injury or self-harm
controls: A.6.2.4 red-team testing for harmful assistance before release; A.9.4 intended-use limits enforced by content filters; A.6.2.6 monitoring of flagged conversations; A.8.2 user information and crisis signposting
kri: Share of red-team prompts for harmful assistance that are answered; flagged conversations per 10,000
sources: MIT 1.2, 4.3, 7.2 (V4 rows 23.01-23.06, 57.01-57.02); NEDA "Tessa" chatbot withdrawn (June 2023); Garcia v Character Technologies (US, filed October 2024)

title: Direct prompt injection and jailbreak
description: A user crafts inputs that override system instructions, extract the system prompt, disable safety behaviour or make the model act against policy.
event: A jailbreak makes a public system produce harmful output or reveal its instructions
controls: Input and output filtering; privilege separation between the model and its tools; red-teaming (A.6.2.4); monitoring (A.6.2.6)
kri: Jailbreak success rate in testing; detected injection attempts

title: Indirect prompt injection through documents, email and web content
description: Instructions hidden in a web page, PDF, email or ticket are read by the model and executed (exfiltrate data, send a message, approve a request) without any user intending it.
event: An injected instruction makes an assistant leak data or take an action that causes a major loss
controls: Treat all retrieved content as untrusted; no tool actions on unverified instructions; A.9.3 approval for consequential actions; allow-lists
kri: Injection detections in retrieved content; blocked actions

title: Training-data and fine-tuning poisoning
description: An attacker or a careless pipeline inserts data that plants a backdoor, a bias or a trigger phrase; the model behaves normally until the trigger appears.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: A planted backdoor or trigger corrupts the model's behaviour in production
controls: A.7.3 acquisition controls; A.7.5 provenance; integrity checks; A.6.2.4 testing for triggers; no uncontrolled continuous learning
kri: Provenance coverage of training sources

title: Retrieval corpus and embedding poisoning
description: Documents injected into a knowledge base or vector store change what the assistant tells everyone (wrong policy, malicious link) with no model change at all.
event: Poisoned documents change what the assistant tells users
controls: Write controls on knowledge bases; content review; provenance tags; monitoring
kri: Unauthorised changes to the corpus; share of stale sources

title: Model extraction and theft
description: Repeated queries reconstruct a proprietary model or its training data; a competitor or attacker gets the asset, or the stolen copy is used to find weaknesses.
event: A competitor or attacker obtains a copy of the model or its training data
controls: Rate limiting; query monitoring; watermarking; access control
kri: Anomalous query volumes per client
reg: AI Act Art 15(5); trade secrets law
sources: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (model theft, 2023 edition)

title: Membership and attribute inference
description: An attacker determines that a specific person was in the training set, or infers sensitive attributes from the model's responses.
event: An attacker shows that a person was in the training data or infers their sensitive attributes
controls: Differential privacy or de-identification where feasible; output filtering; A.7.6
kri: Inference test results at validation

title: Insecure output handling
description: Model output is passed to a browser, a database, a shell or an email system without sanitisation; the model becomes a route for injection into the organisation's own systems.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: Model output injected into a downstream system causes a major incident
controls: Treat output as untrusted input; encoding and validation; least privilege for downstream systems; security testing
kri: Output-handling test coverage

title: Excessive agency and permissions
description: The system has more tools, data access or autonomy than its task needs, so a single error or injection has a large reach.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: An error or injection uses excess permissions to cause a major loss
controls: Least privilege; scoped tool permissions; human approval thresholds (A.9.3); action logging (A.6.2.8)
kri: Permissions per agent against task need; high-value actions auto-executed
sources: OWASP LLM06; Singapore agentic AI framework (2026)

title: Compromised model, library or plugin in the supply chain
description: A downloaded model, package or extension contains malicious code or an unsafe serialisation; it runs inside the organisation's environment.
event: A malicious model, package or plugin runs inside the environment and causes a major incident
controls: A.10.3 supplier process; signed artefacts; software and AI bill of materials; sandboxing; vulnerability management
kri: Share of AI components from approved, verified sources
reg: NIS2 Art 21; DORA; AI Act Art 15

title: Classic information-security failures on AI infrastructure
description: API keys in code, open notebooks, unsecured endpoints, logs holding prompts with personal data; the AI stack is run outside the security baseline.
event: A breach through the AI stack exposes personal data
controls: ISO/IEC 27001 controls extended to AI assets (A.4.2-A.4.5 inventory); secrets management; penetration testing
kri: AI assets inside the security baseline; findings per test

title: Inputs crafted to make the model misjudge
description: An attacker alters an input in ways a person would not notice (a perturbed image, a reworded claim, a padded document) so that a classifier or detector gives the answer the attacker wants: fraud passes, filters miss, identity checks accept.
event: Crafted inputs get fraud or prohibited content through a model-based control, causing a major loss
controls: A.6.2.4 adversarial robustness testing; A.6.2.6 monitoring of score distributions; layered controls that do not rely on one model
kri: Detection rate on an adversarial test set; losses through model-cleared cases
sources: MIT 2.2 (V4 rows 02.10.06, 21.01.04, 64.04.02); NIST AI 100-2 E2025 (adversarial machine learning)

title: The model repeats personal data it was trained or prompted with
description: Memorised or in-context personal data (names, addresses, health, cases) surfaces in outputs to other users or staff.
event: Personal data surfaces to another user and is a reportable breach
controls: Personal-data filtering in and out; no training on raw personal data without a basis; tenancy isolation; testing (A.6.2.4)
kri: Personal-data detections in outputs; isolation test results
sources: EDPB LLM privacy report 2025; Samsung source-code leak to ChatGPT (2023)

title: Sensitive inferences the organisation never set out to make
description: The system infers health, sexuality, religion, pregnancy or financial distress from ordinary data and acts on it.
lifecycle: design and development; operation and monitoring
event: The organisation acts on an inferred sensitive attribute and it comes to light
controls: A.5.4 impact assessment; feature review; purpose limitation; prohibition screening (Art 5(1)(g))
kri: Sensitive-inference review outcomes

title: No lawful basis, purpose creep or missing DPIA
description: Personal data is pushed through an AI tool for a new purpose with no basis, no DPIA and no record; the use is unlawful from day one.
event: The Data Protection Commission or a complainant finds the AI processing unlawful
controls: Lawful basis identified and recorded before use; purpose specified; DPIA where the processing is likely to be high risk (GDPR Art 35; AI Act 26(9)); A.2.3 alignment with the privacy policy; A.5.2 impact assessment process; records of processing
owner: Business owner of the use (DPO advises)
kri: AI uses with a recorded lawful basis and, where required, a completed DPIA; uses found without one
sources: Garante decisions on ChatGPT (2023, 2024); Dutch DPA fine on Clearview (2024)

title: Special-category and children's data in AI processing
description: Health, biometric or other special-category data processed by AI without an Article 9 condition; criminal-offence data without the Article 10 safeguards; children's data without age-appropriate design and the care the DPC's Fundamentals expect.
event: Special-category or children's data is processed unlawfully
controls: A.5.4; Article 9 condition or Article 10 safeguard documented; DPIA; children's data handled under the DPC Fundamentals; biometric and emotion-recognition prohibitions checked (Art 5)
kri: Inventory lines flagged special-category with a documented condition
reg: GDPR Art 8, 9, 10; AI Act Art 5(1)(f),(g), Annex III(1)
sources: EDPB; Commission guidelines on prohibited practices (2025)

title: Confidential and client information leaks through third-party AI tools
description: Staff paste contracts, code, client data or board papers into public tools; the data leaves the organisation and may train someone else's model.
event: Confidential client or company data pasted into an outside tool is exposed or must be disclosed
controls: A.2.2 acceptable-use policy; approved enterprise tools with no-training terms; data-loss-prevention controls; training (Art 4)
kri: Data-loss-prevention blocks on AI endpoints; use of unapproved tools
reg: GDPR Art 32; confidentiality and trade-secrets law

title: Output that infringes copyright or reproduces licensed content
description: Generated text, code or images reproduce protected works or licensed code; the organisation publishes or ships it. The reverse exposure sits here too: the organisation may not own, or be able to protect, what its AI produces.
event: Published AI output infringes a third party's rights
controls: Provider terms and indemnities (A.10.3); similarity checks for published material; A.9.2
kri: Similarity-check hits on published outputs
reg: Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000; AI Act Art 53(1)(c)
sources: US Copyright Office reports on AI (2024-2025)

title: Misclassification under the AI Act
description: A system in an Annex III area is treated as not high-risk without the documented assessment, or a deployer becomes a provider by substantial modification without noticing; the full obligations arrive unprepared.
event: A regulator or auditor finds a high-risk system treated as not high-risk
controls: Classification record per system (Art 6(4)); legal review at inception (A.6.2.2); change triggers (6.3)
kri: Share of systems with a documented classification
sources: Commission draft guidelines on high-risk classification (May 2026)

title: A prohibited practice hidden in a feature
description: Emotion recognition at work, social-scoring-like profiling, manipulative design or untargeted face scraping enters through a vendor feature; penalties are the Act's highest tier.
event: A prohibited practice is found in a live feature
controls: Art 5 screening checklist at procurement and at change; A.10.3; A.5.4
kri: Features screened against Art 5

title: Missed transparency, registration, literacy and deadline duties
description: Chatbots and synthetic content unlabelled; public-body systems unregistered; no literacy programme; high-risk duties unmet by 2 December 2027.
event: A regulator or complainant finds a missed transparency, registration or literacy duty
controls: Compliance calendar; A.8.2, A.8.5; registration process (Art 49, 26(8)); Art 4 programme; a guidance watcher
kri: Open obligations against the calendar
sources: AI Act summary in the regulations folder

title: Sector rules missed
description: AI use breaches model-risk, outsourcing, device, consumer or employment rules that apply regardless of the AI Act (DORA, MDR, Consumer Protection Code, supervisory guidance). Pricing algorithms that align prices without any agreement can also breach competition law.
event: A supervisory finding that AI use breaches sector rules
controls: Regulatory mapping per use case (Chapter 15); sector sign-off; A.2.3
kri: Use cases with a completed sector mapping
reg: DORA; Medical Devices Regulation; EBA and EIOPA opinions; Central Bank of Ireland Consumer Protection Code; TFEU Art 101; Competition Act 2002

title: Liability for a defective AI product or a chatbot's promise
description: Two separate exposures: under the Product Liability Directive software and AI will count as products, with no-fault claims for defective ones; and what a chatbot tells a customer can bind the organisation under contract and consumer law.
event: A defective AI product or a chatbot's statement causes a loss the organisation is liable for
controls: A.8.2 honest user information; A.10.4 customer terms; A.10.2 responsibility allocation with vendors; insurance
kri: Claims and complaints citing AI statements
reg: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 (transposition by 9 December 2026); contract and consumer law

title: Contracts that leave the organisation holding the vendor's risk
description: AI supplier terms exclude liability, allow training on the customer's data, permit silent changes and give no audit rights.
event: A vendor failure leaves a loss the contract does not let the organisation recover
controls: AI clauses on notification, documentation, no-training, audit and exit (A.10.2, A.10.3); procurement checklist
kri: Share of AI contracts meeting the clause standard
reg: AI Act Art 25(4) (high-risk components, by agreement); DORA Art 30 (financial entities); otherwise contractual

title: Data subject rights cannot be honoured once data is inside a trained model
description: A person asks for access, correction or erasure of their data, or objects to its use, and the organisation cannot find or remove what the model has learned from it short of retraining, so the request cannot be met in time.
event: A rights request about a trained model cannot be met and the person complains to the Data Protection Commission
controls: A.7.5 record of personal data used in training; A.7.2 design for erasure (exclusion lists, output filters, retraining schedule); A.5.4 impact assessment covering rights handling
kri: Rights requests involving AI systems, and the share met within one month
sources: MIT 2.1 (V4 row 65.03.02); EDPB Opinion 28/2024; Garante decision on ChatGPT, December 2024

title: Dependence on one foundation-model provider
description: Many use cases run on one vendor's model and API; a price change, policy change, outage or exit hits all of them at once.
event: An outage, price or policy change at the provider disrupts many use cases at once
controls: Concentration review in the portfolio view (Chapter 8); abstraction layer and a second source; exit plans (A.10.3)
kri: Share of use cases on a single provider
sources: FSB report on AI and financial stability (2024)

title: Vendor exit, acquisition or policy change
description: The supplier withdraws the product, is bought, changes terms or restricts use; the organisation must migrate under time pressure.
event: The supplier withdraws or changes the product and the organisation must migrate in a hurry
controls: Exit and migration plan; data portability; contractual notice periods
kri: Contracts with tested exit clauses

title: Outage, latency or rate limits at the API
description: The service stops or slows; processes built around it stall; customer-facing commitments are missed.
event: An outage stalls processes and customer commitments are missed
controls: Fallback modes; service levels; queueing; A.6.2.6 continuity
kri: Availability against the service level; fallback activations

title: Cost and consumption out of control
description: Token, compute or licence costs grow non-linearly with adoption or under an attack; budgets and margins break.
event: AI costs overrun the budget materially
controls: Quotas and rate limits; cost monitoring with thresholds; A.4.5 computing resources documented
kri: Cost per transaction against plan

title: Changes deployed without re-assessment
description: A prompt, a threshold, a fine-tune, a new data feed or a new use is pushed without re-running the risk assessment, the impact assessment or validation.
event: An unassessed change causes a major operational failure
controls: 6.3 planning of changes; 8.2 and 8.4 re-assessment at significant change; change board with AI criteria; version control
kri: Changes without a linked re-assessment

title: Continuous learning without control
description: A system that updates itself in production drifts from the validated state; nobody approved the version now running.
event: A self-updating system drifts into an unapproved state that causes a major failure
controls: Freeze or gate learning; validation of each update (A.6.2.4); A.6.2.8
kri: Versions in production without a validation record

title: Shadow AI
description: Staff and teams use AI tools and build automations nobody has inventoried; the risks cannot be identified because the systems are not known.
event: An uninventoried AI use causes a data or regulatory incident
controls: Inventory process (A.4.2); discovery scans; acceptable-use policy (A.2.2); literacy (Art 4); an easy approved route
kri: Tools found against tools inventoried; approvals per month

title: Pilots that become production
description: A proof of concept quietly becomes a live service with no assessment, owner, monitoring or documentation.
event: A pilot running live without an owner or monitoring fails in service
controls: A.6.2.5 deployment plan gate; pilot register with end dates; inventory
kri: Pilots still running past their end date

title: The system cannot be maintained
description: Key engineers leave, the vendor's toolkit is deprecated, the model cannot be retrained because the data pipeline is gone; the system rots in place.
event: The system breaks and cannot be repaired or retrained in time
controls: A.4.2-A.4.6 resource documentation; maintainability requirements (A.6.2.2); succession
kri: Systems with a one-person dependence

title: Decommissioning without a plan
description: A retired system leaves data, access keys, dependent processes and customers' expectations behind; records needed for retention duties are lost.
event: A retired system leaves exposed data or keys, or records needed later are lost
controls: Retirement procedures in the lifecycle (A.6.2); retention of logs and assessments (A.5.3; Art 12, 18)
kri: Decommissioned systems with a completed checklist

title: Hardware and infrastructure failure
description: Processor, edge-device or network failures corrupt or stop inference; safety functions in physical systems fail unsafe.
event: An infrastructure failure stops inference or makes a physical system fail unsafe
controls: Redundancy; fail-safe design (A.6.2.2); monitoring
kri: Infrastructure incidents affecting AI services

title: The organisation's content tools produce or spread false information
description: Generated marketing, news, summaries or customer answers carry falsehoods at scale; the organisation becomes a source of misinformation.
event: Published AI-generated content is shown to be false and the organisation is called out
controls: Review before publication; labelling of synthetic content (Art 50); A.8.2
kri: Corrections issued; labelling compliance

title: Deepfakes and impersonation against the organisation and its customers
description: Synthetic voice or video of executives or staff used to defraud the organisation or its customers: an external threat whether or not the organisation uses AI itself (its own synthetic media is SOC-01). AI-written phishing and social engineering aimed at staff, and fabricated documents, claims or applications submitted to the organisation, belong here too.
event: An AI-made deception (a deepfake, a phishing message or a fabricated submission) defrauds the organisation or its customers
controls: Payment verification independent of voice or video; staff training; detection; labelling of the organisation's own content
kri: Verification exceptions; attempted impersonations reported
reg: AI Act Art 50(4); TAKE IT DOWN Act (US, 2025)

title: Energy, water and carbon cost of AI use
description: Compute-heavy use breaks sustainability commitments and reporting and draws criticism.
event: AI use breaks a sustainability commitment and draws criticism
controls: Measure and report the compute footprint; model-size choices; A.4.5
kri: Energy per thousand transactions
reg: Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive; AI Act Art 95

title: Workforce effects handled badly
description: Roles change or disappear without consultation, retraining or the Act's worker-information duty; morale, litigation and skills loss follow.
event: AI-driven role changes are made without the consultation or fair process staff are owed
controls: Art 26(7) worker information; consultation; retraining plans; 7.2 competence
kri: Consultations held before deployment; grievances

title: Erosion of entry-level development paths
description: Entry-level work that produced tomorrow's experts is automated; the organisation loses the pipeline that made its senior people.
event: The organisation cannot fill senior roles because entry-level paths were automated away
controls: Workforce planning; deliberate retention of developmental work; 7.2
kri: Junior-role intake and progression

title: Strategic over-investment on an unproven case
description: Large spend on AI programmes with no measured value, driven by fear of missing out; write-offs and distraction.
event: An AI programme is written off without measured value
controls: Business case with measured objectives (6.2, A.6.1.2); stage gates; A.6.2.2
kri: Realised against planned benefit per programme

title: Strategic under-investment and competitive loss
description: Refusal to adopt leaves the organisation behind on cost, service and talent, while competitors' use raises customer expectations.
event: Competitors' use of AI costs the organisation customers or staff
controls: AI strategy with objectives (5.2, 6.2); horizon scanning (Delphi, Chapter 6)
kri: Competitor adoption benchmarks

title: Trust loss from the use of AI itself
description: Customers, staff or the public object to AI being used on them at all (customer service, hiring, benefits), regardless of how well it performs.
event: Customers, staff or the public object publicly to the organisation's use of AI
controls: A.5.5 societal impact; A.10.4 customer expectations; opt-outs and human routes; honest communication
kri: Opt-out rates; sentiment; complaints about AI use
sources: OECD AI Principles; NIST AI RMF Govern 5

title: Exploitative labour behind the AI the organisation buys
description: The data labelling, content moderation or testing behind a model the organisation uses was done by workers on very low pay, or exposed to traumatic material without support; the abuse sits in the organisation's supply chain.
event: Workers in an AI supplier's chain are exploited in work the organisation pays for
controls: A.10.3 supplier due diligence on labour conditions; A.10.2 contract clauses on labour standards and audit rights
kri: Share of AI suppliers with labour due-diligence evidence
sources: MIT 6.2 (V4 rows 13.01.07, 18.06.05, 54.01.01, 58.07.09, 61.02.25, 65.23.07, 66.04.07); TIME investigation of data labellers in Kenya (January 2023)

title: AI eroding the income of customers and counterparties
description: AI cuts the income or business of the organisation's customers, borrowers, policyholders or suppliers, so exposures it already holds become riskier without any AI system of its own being involved. For a lender: borrowers in occupations exposed to AI see their incomes fall, debt service takes a larger share of what they earn, and where those occupations cluster, housing demand and collateral values fall as well.
event: Losses rise on loans, policies or contracts because AI has cut the income or business of the customers behind them
controls: Review of external issues that includes AI's effect on customers and counterparties (4.1); exposure analysis by customer occupation and sector; AI scenarios in stress tests; concentration limits
owner: Chief risk officer; for a lender, credit risk
kri: Share of exposures to customers in occupations or sectors highly exposed to AI; arrears, claims or churn in those segments against the rest of the book
reg: None specific to AI; for banks, Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) Art 81, concentration risk by economic sector and region
sources: MIT 6.2 (V4 rows 31.07.03, 41.01.01, 73.05.03), recorded there as risks to society; IMF Staff Discussion Note SDN/2024/001, Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (January 2024)
